title: The Roman–Sasanian World
subtitle: 224–632 · Two Empires and Their Frontier: Shapur and Valerian, the Peace of Nisibis, Justinian and Khusrau, the Last Great War and the Arab Conquests' Threshold

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: Ardashir, Shapur I and II, Kavad and the two Khusraus; Valerian, Diocletian, Julian, Justinian, Maurice and Heraclius; the Arab clients and the vassal kings

entries.label: Ardashir I and the founding of the Sasanian state
entries.hint: Ardashir, ruler of Fars, defeated the last Arsacid at Hormizdagan in 224, was crowned in 226 and by 230 had taken the old Parthian lands to the Euphrates, with new capitals at Ardashir-Khwarra (Firuzabad) and Ctesiphon, and the title Shahanshah, King of Kings of the Iranians; he built a centralised state with the Zoroastrian priesthood as its ally, and attacked Roman Mesopotamia in 230–232.
entries.note: Tabari, History; Touraj Daryaee, Sasanian Persia (2009); Josef Wiesehöfer, Ancient Persia (1996).

entries.label: Shapur I
entries.hint: Shapur I, who succeeded his father Ardashir, invaded Syria in 252–253 and 256, sacked Antioch and Dura-Europos, defeated and captured the emperor Valerian in 260, left a trilingual inscription of his deeds (Res Gestae Divi Saporis) on the Ka'ba-ye Zardosht at Naqsh-e Rostam, founded Bishapur and Gundeshapur with Roman prisoners and gave Mani leave to teach.
entries.note: Res Gestae Divi Saporis (ŠKZ); Michael Back; Daryaee 2009; Ammianus 23.5; Lactantius, De mortibus persecutorum 5.

entries.label: Shapur II
entries.hint: Shapur II, king from before his birth, who was crowned as an infant in 309 and ruled for seventy years, put down the Arab raiders, took Armenia, besieged Nisibis three times, fought a long war with Constantius II in 337–361 and, in the war of Julian's invasion of 363, forced Jovian to cede Nisibis and the five provinces, and presided over the compiling of the Avesta and the persecutions of the Christians.
entries.note: Ammianus Marcellinus 16–25; Tabari; Daryaee 2009; Richard Frye, in The Cambridge History of Iran vol. 3 (1983).

entries.label: Kavad I and Khusrau I Anushirvan
entries.hint: Kavad I, restored by the Hephthalites after being deposed in 496, fought Anastasius in 502–506 and Justin in 524–531 and patronised the communist-leaning Mazdak movement before turning on it; his son Khusrau I (531–579) reformed the taxation and army with a cadastral survey, the dihgans' service, the Eternal Peace of 532, the sack of Antioch in 540, the conquests in Yemen and Lazica and the cultural revival with Greek and Indian learning.
entries.note: Procopius, Wars 1–2; Agathias; Tabari; Daryaee 2009; Parvaneh Pourshariati, Decline and Fall of the Sasanian Empire (2008).

entries.label: Khusrau II Parvez
entries.hint: Khusrau II, restored to the throne in 591 by the emperor Maurice after the usurpation of Bahram Chobin, swore revenge when Maurice was murdered by Phocas in 602, and conquered Mesopotamia, Syria, Palestine and Egypt, reached Chalcedon in 617 and 626, built the great palace of Dastagird and amassed gold and treasures; after Heraclius' invasion he was deposed and killed by his son Kavad II in February 628.
entries.note: Theophylact Simocatta; Sebeos; Chronicon Paschale; Theophanes; James Howard-Johnston, Witnesses to a World Crisis (2010).

entries.label: Diocletian and Galerius
entries.hint: Diocletian, an Illyrian soldier who took the throne in 284 and divided power in the Tetrarchy, made the East his own, strengthened the Strata Diocletiana and the limes of Syria, Mesopotamia and Arabia; Galerius, his Caesar, was defeated by Narseh in 296 near Carrhae but crushed him in 298, captured his harem and treasure, and in the Peace of Nisibis of 299 took five trans-Tigrine provinces and the protectorate of Armenia and Iberia.
entries.note: Peter the Patrician, fr. 13–14; Ammianus; Fergus Millar, The Roman Near East 31 BC–AD 337 (1993); Timothy Barnes, Constantine and Eusebius (1981).

entries.label: Constantine and Constantius II
entries.hint: Constantine, after the defeat of his rivals in 324, set himself up as protector of the Christians of Persia and prepared an eastern campaign for 337, when he died at Nicomedia; his son Constantius II fought the Persians in a series of inconclusive wars and sieges of Nisibis (338, 346, 350) while the Sasanians attacked Roman Mesopotamia, Singara and Amida in 359.
entries.note: Eusebius, Vita Constantini 4.8–13; Ammianus 18–19; Barnes 1981; Michael Whitby in The Cambridge Ancient History vol. 13 (1998).

entries.label: Justinian and Theodora
entries.hint: Justinian, who restored the western provinces by his generals Belisarius and Narses and codified the law, fought Persia in 527–532 and 540–562 with the dual aims of securing the eastern frontier and of using peace payments to free his armies; the Eternal Peace of 532 and the Fifty Years' Peace of 562, in which he agreed to pay 30,000 gold coins a year, left him free in Italy.
entries.note: Procopius, Wars 1–2, Secret History; Menander the Guardsman; Geoffrey Greatrex and Samuel Lieu, The Roman Eastern Frontier and the Persian Wars vol. 2 (2002).

entries.label: Maurice, Phocas and Heraclius
entries.hint: Maurice (582–602), who put Khusrau II on the throne and gained Armenia, was murdered with his sons by Phocas, whose tyranny set off the Persian invasion; Heraclius, son of the exarch of Africa, overthrew Phocas in 610, was almost beaten in 618–622, then led the campaigns of 622–628 that brought Khusrau's fall, and restored the Cross in Jerusalem in 630.
entries.note: Theophylact; Chronicon Paschale; Walter Kaegi, Heraclius, Emperor of Byzantium (2003); Howard-Johnston 2010.

entries.label: The Lakhmids of al-Hira and the Ghassanids
entries.hint: The Lakhmid kings of al-Hira, such as al-Mundhir III (505–554), who was killed in battle by the Ghassanids in 554, were clients of Persia, patrons of poetry and Christians of the Church of the East; the Ghassanid phylarchs, led by al-Harith ibn Jabala (529–569) and al-Mundhir (569–582), were the empire's Miaphysite Arab allies, whose fall in 582 and the Lakhmids' end in 602 removed the buffer states before the Arab conquests.
entries.note: Procopius, Wars 1–2; John of Ephesus; Irfan Shahid, Byzantium and the Arabs vols. 1–3 (1984–1995); Ibn al-Kalbi.
keywords: Christians of the Church of the East

entries.label: Armenia, Iberia and Albania in the two empires
entries.hint: Armenia, Iberia and Albania, which had been Arsacid and Roman-aligned, were divided between Sasanian and Roman influence by the partition of 387, with the larger share to Persia; the Sasanians' attempts to force Zoroastrianism led to the rising of Vardan Mamikonian at Avarayr in 451, which led to the religious freedom granted in the Treaty of Nvarsak in 484, while the Roman emperors used Armenia and Lazica for recruiting soldiers.
entries.note: Elishe, History of Vardan and the Armenian War; Lazar of P'arpi; Nina Garsoïan in The Armenian People vol. 1 (1997); Cyril Toumanoff, Studies in Christian Caucasian History (1963).

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: Edessa 260, Nisibis, Ctesiphon 363, the wars of Justinian, the Antioch sack of 540 and the war of 602–628

entries.label: The capture of Valerian
entries.hint: In 260 Shapur I defeated the Roman army near Edessa and captured the emperor Valerian, with the Praetorian Prefect and many senators; the emperor's humiliation, shown on the rock reliefs of Naqsh-e Rostam, Bishapur and Darabgird, in which Philip the Arab kneels and Valerian is taken by the wrist, is the single largest disaster of a Roman emperor, and he died in captivity, as Lactantius says, flayed and stuffed.
entries.note: Res Gestae Divi Saporis 18–22; Lactantius, De mortibus 5; Zosimus 1.36; Naqsh-e Rostam and Bishapur reliefs; Michael Whitby, Rome at War (2002).

entries.label: Odaenathus, Zenobia and Aurelian
entries.hint: After Valerian's capture Odaenathus, the lord of Palmyra, drove the Persians back from Roman territory in 262–267 and was granted a Roman command of the East; his widow Zenobia took Egypt and Anatolia in 270–271 and declared her son Vaballathus Augustus, until Aurelian defeated her at Antioch and Emesa in 272 and razed Palmyra after a revolt in 273.
entries.note: Zosimus 1.39–61; Historia Augusta, Tyranni Triginta; Palmyrene inscriptions; Pat Southern, Empress Zenobia (2008).

entries.label: Narseh's war and the Peace of Nisibis
entries.hint: Narseh, who had seized the throne from Bahram III and lost Armenia, attacked in 296 and defeated Galerius between Carrhae and Callinicum, but in 298 Galerius surprised his camp in Armenia, wounding the king and taking his wives, sisters and children; the Peace of Nisibis, negotiated in 299 by the diplomats Sicorius Probus and Apharban, gave Rome five trans-Tigritane satrapies and the right to name the king of Iberia.
entries.note: Peter the Patrician fr. 14; Paikuli inscription; Eutropius 9.24–25; Ammianus 25.7.9; Barnes 1981.

entries.label: Julian's Persian expedition
entries.hint: Julian led an army of 65,000 down the Euphrates in March 363 and reached Ctesiphon, burned his ships and moved up the Tigris instead of attacking the capital; he was killed in a skirmish near Samarra on 26 June, probably by a Persian spear, and his successor Jovian, with a starving army, ceded Nisibis, Singara and the five provinces to Shapur II in a peace of thirty years.
entries.note: Ammianus 23–25; Libanius, Orations 17–18; Zosimus 3; Gregory Nazianzen, Orations 4–5; Glen Bowersock, Julian the Apostate (1978).

entries.label: The siege of Amida and the Anastasian war
entries.hint: Kavad I, claiming unpaid subsidies for the defence of the Caspian Gates, took Theodosiopolis in 502 and Amida in January 503 after a siege of three months; Anastasius sent armies, and after three years of fighting the two sides made a seven-year truce in 506, with the Romans building the fortress of Dara in 505–507 on the border, a cause of the dispute for years.
entries.note: Joshua the Stylite, Chronicle; Procopius, Wars 1.7–10; Greatrex and Lieu 2002.

entries.label: The sack of Antioch
entries.hint: Khusrau I broke the Eternal Peace in 540, took Sura, Beroea and Hierapolis and in June besieged Antioch, taking the third city of the empire after a short assault, plundering its churches, taking thousands of its people to found a new city, Veh Antiok Khusrau (Rumagan), near Ctesiphon, and collecting large sums of gold from the cities of Syria and Mesopotamia.
entries.note: Procopius, Wars 2.5–14; Malalas 17; Evagrius, Ecclesiastical History 4.25–26; Greatrex and Lieu 2002.

entries.label: The Lazic war
entries.hint: The kingdom of Lazica on the east coast of the Black Sea, a Roman client, passed in 541 to Persian protection, and in a war of two decades the Romans and Persians fought for Petra, Archaeopolis and the passes, on the road to the Caspian; the war ended in the Fifty Years' Peace of 562, which left Lazica to the Romans for a payment of 30,000 solidi a year.
entries.note: Procopius, Wars 2.15–30, 8; Agathias 2–4; Menander fr. 6; Greatrex and Lieu 2002.

entries.label: The Persian conquests of the East
entries.hint: Under Khusrau II's generals Shahrbaraz, Shahin and Farrukhan, Persian armies took Antioch in 611, Damascus in 613, Jerusalem in May 614 with a massacre of the Christians, as the Chronicle of Sebeos and Strategios record, and carried off the True Cross, and Alexandria in 619, Egypt's last Roman city, and Chalcedon opposite Constantinople in 617; the Persian empire reached the extent of the Achaemenids.
entries.note: Sebeos; Strategios of Mar Saba; Chronicon Paschale; John of Nikiu; Howard-Johnston 2010; Kaegi 2003.

entries.label: Heraclius' campaigns and the battle of Nineveh
entries.hint: Heraclius, having made peace with the Avars, led an army through the Black Sea to Armenia and the Caucasus in 622–624 and then in 627, with Turkic Khazar allies, moved into Mesopotamia, defeated the Persian general Rhahzadh at Nineveh on 12 December 627 and marched on Dastagird, plundering the palace; Khusrau fled and was killed in February 628, and his son Kavad II made peace, restoring all the territories.
entries.note: Theophanes AM 6113–6120; George of Pisidia, Heraclias; Kaegi 2003; Howard-Johnston 2010.

entries.label: The siege of Constantinople
entries.hint: In the summer of 626 a Persian army under Shahrbaraz at Chalcedon and an Avar-Slav-Bulgar force of the khagan before the Theodosian walls besieged Constantinople; under the patriarch Sergius and Bonus the city, with the icon of the Virgin carried on the walls, resisted for ten days, and on 7–8 August the Avar fleet of dugouts was destroyed in the Golden Horn and the allies left; the failure marked a turning-point of the war.
entries.note: Chronicon Paschale 716–726; Theodore Synkellos; George of Pisidia, Bellum Avaricum; James Howard-Johnston, Witnesses to a World Crisis (2010).

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The Sasanian state and its church, the Roman diocesan frontier, the treaties of 299, 363, 532 and 562 and the Persian marcher lords

entries.label: The Sasanian state and the four-fold order
entries.hint: The Sasanian state, as it appears in Persian traditions recorded in Arabic and Middle Persian texts, was a hierarchy of a king of kings, the great houses and a landed gentry (dihqans) with an army of cavalry, with four estates of priests, warriors, scribes and commoners; Khusrau I's reform divided the empire into four military quarters under spahbeds, fixed a land and poll tax, and set up a bureaucracy of the royal secretaries.
entries.note: Tabari; Letter of Tansar; Ibn al-Muqaffa'; Pourshariati 2008; Daryaee 2009.

entries.label: The Roman diocese and the frontier army
entries.hint: Diocletian divided the East into dioceses of Oriens and Egypt under the praetorian prefect and a duke on each frontier sector, with a field army (comitatenses) under the master of soldiers and the limitanei in the forts; in the sixth century Justinian made the dukes of Mesopotamia, Armenia and Phoenicia responsible for fortifications, and set up a magister militum per Armeniam.
entries.note: Notitia Dignitatum; Codex Justinianus; A. H. M. Jones, The Later Roman Empire (1964); Whitby 2002.

entries.label: The Peace of Jovian
entries.hint: Jovian, to bring his starving army back, concluded in July 363 a thirty years' truce, ceding the five trans-Tigrine provinces taken in 298, including the great fortress city of Nisibis, which was evacuated by its citizens, with Singara and Castra Maurorum, and abandoning Armenia to Persian influence; some contemporaries and later writers likened the humiliation to the Caudine Forks.
entries.note: Ammianus 25.7–9; Zosimus 3.31; Libanius, Oration 18; Whitby 2002.

entries.label: The Eternal Peace and the Fifty Years' Peace
entries.hint: In 532 the emperor Justinian, to free his hands for the West, made an Eternal Peace with Khusrau I and paid 11,000 pounds of gold; after the war of 540–561 a fifty years' treaty in 562, negotiated by Peter the Patrician and Zich, allowed the Persians a payment of 30,000 solidi a year, stopped Persian interference in the Roman Armenia and Lazica, and set out a long list of trade, religion and diplomatic rights in the text recorded by Menander.
entries.note: Procopius, Wars 1.22; Menander the Guardsman fr. 6; Greatrex and Lieu 2002.

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: Zoroastrian orthodoxy, Mani, the Persian martyrs, the Church of the East, the Talmud and Mazdak

entries.label: The Babylonian Talmud
entries.hint: The Jewish academies of Sura, Pumbedita and Nehardea, under the exilarch, developed the Babylonian Talmud, a great commentary on the Mishnah, in generations of rabbis from Rav and Samuel in the early third century to Ravina and Rav Ashi in the fifth, and its final redaction by the saboraim in the sixth; the Persian kings were mostly tolerant, with an occasional persecution, as under Yazdgerd II and Peroz.
entries.note: Babylonian Talmud; Jacob Neusner, A History of the Jews in Babylonia vols. 2–5 (1966–1970); Isaiah Gafni.

entries.label: Mani and Manichaeism
entries.hint: Mani, born in Babylonia in 216 to a Parthian family and raised in a baptising sect, proclaimed himself the Seal of the Prophets in 240, was patronised by Shapur I, wrote the Shabuhragan for him and sent missionaries to the Roman empire, India and Central Asia; he was imprisoned and died in Gundeshapur about 276 under Bahram I, but his religion spread across Eurasia and lasted to the sixteenth century.
entries.note: Cologne Mani Codex; Kephalaia; Iain Gardner and Samuel Lieu, Manichaean Texts from the Roman Empire (2004); Samuel Lieu, Manichaeism in Mesopotamia and the Roman East (1994).

entries.label: Kartir and the Zoroastrian church
entries.hint: The priest Kartir, adviser to Shapur I, Hormizd I, Bahram I and II, and grand mobed, set up fire temples throughout the empire and, in his inscriptions on the Ka'ba-ye Zardosht and at Naqsh-e Rajab, boasts of having persecuted Jews, Buddhists, Hindus, Nazarenes, Christians, baptisers and Manichaeans; the death of Mani about 276 was his work.
entries.note: Kartir's inscriptions (KKZ, KNRm, KSM); Mary Boyce, A History of Zoroastrianism vol. 3 (1991); David Neil MacKenzie, ‘Kerdir's Inscription’ (1989).

entries.label: The Persian martyrs and the Church of the East
entries.hint: The Christians of Persia, deportees from Roman Syria and Mesopotamia and native converts, were suspected as a fifth column of Rome, and under Shapur II in the Forty Years' Persecution, from 339, the catholicos Simeon bar Sabbae was executed and tens of thousands were killed; the Synod of Isaac in 410 organised the Church of the East under a catholicos of Seleucia-Ctesiphon, which became Nestorian in 486 and 497.
entries.note: Acts of the Persian Martyrs; Synodicon Orientale (ed. Chabot, 1902); Sebastian Brock, ‘Christians in the Sasanian Empire’ (1982); Aphrahat, Demonstrations.

entries.label: Mazdak and the Zoroastrian reform
entries.hint: Mazdak, a priest who taught that the wealth, women and property of the rich should be held in common to end the strife, had the support of Kavad I in the 490s, which turned the nobility and clergy against the king, who was deposed in 496; Khusrau I, with Zoroastrian orthodoxy, suppressed the sect in 528 and killed its leaders.
entries.note: Tabari; Nizam al-Mulk, Siyasatnama; Patricia Crone, ‘Kavad's Heresy and Mazdak's Revolt’, Iran 29 (1991).

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: Shapur's rock reliefs, the silverware, Taq-e Kasra and the churches of Syria and Mesopotamia

entries.label: The rock reliefs of Shapur
entries.hint: Shapur I and his successors carved on the cliffs of Naqsh-e Rostam, Bishapur and Darabgird the triumph over Rome: Valerian is led by the wrist, Gordian III lies beneath the horse and Philip the Arab kneels, in reliefs that show the king as the equal of the Achaemenids, whose tombs are on the same cliff, and which recall the defeat in a monumental form that Rome's reliefs did not.
entries.note: Bishapur reliefs; Naqsh-e Rostam; Georgina Herrmann, The Iranian Revival (1977); Matthew Canepa, The Two Eyes of the Earth (2009).

entries.label: The silverware of the Sasanian court
entries.hint: Gilded silver bowls, plates and ewers with scenes of the king hunting lions, banqueting with musicians and dancers and fighting, struck with the royal stamps and weights of the treasury, were among the best known of the court's products; the Sasanian hunting plates were exported to Central Asia, China and the Byzantine empire, where they were copied.
entries.note: Prudence Harper, Silver Vessels of the Sasanian Period vol. 1 (1981); Daryaee 2009; British Museum and Hermitage holdings.

entries.label: Ephrem, Narsai and the Syriac hymn
entries.hint: Ephrem the Syrian (c. 306–373), deacon of Nisibis and then of Edessa after its cession in 363, wrote hymns, commentaries and homilies in Syriac that made him the greatest poet of Syriac Christianity; Narsai (d. 502), the head of the school of Nisibis, and Jacob of Serugh composed verse homilies, and the Syriac of Mesopotamia became a literary language of the church across the Roman and Persian frontier.
entries.note: Ephrem, Hymns on Paradise, Carmina Nisibena; Sebastian Brock, The Luminous Eye (1985); Brock, The Hidden Pearl (2001).

entries.label: Taq-e Kasra and the palace of Ctesiphon
entries.hint: The great iwan of Ctesiphon, usually called Taq-e Kasra, with a vault of 25 metres span and 37 metres high, the widest unreinforced brick vault in the world, built probably under Khusrau I with the prisoners of Antioch or under Khusrau II, was the throne hall of the palace and the model of Persian court architecture; its carpet, the Spring of Khusrau, was taken as plunder by the Arabs in 637.
entries.note: Tabari; Ernst Kühnel, Ctesiphon (1933); Daryaee 2009; Michael Morony, Iraq after the Muslim Conquest (1984).

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: The Academy of Gundeshapur, Persian translations, the Syriac school at Nisibis and Procopius

entries.label: The Academy of Gundeshapur
entries.hint: Gundeshapur, a city founded by Shapur I in Khuzestan with Roman prisoners, held under Khusrau I a medical school and hospital where Greek, Indian and Persian learning was taught, which was joined by the Greek philosophers who left Athens when Justinian closed the Academy in 529, and in the later tradition it was the source of the transmission of Greek medicine to Islam.
entries.note: Tabari; Ibn Abi Usaybi'a, Uyun al-anba; Agathias 2.30–31; Daryaee 2009; Michael Dols, ‘The Origins of the Islamic Hospital’, Bulletin of the History of Medicine 61 (1987).

entries.label: The school of Nisibis
entries.hint: When the Roman city of Nisibis was ceded to Persia in 363, its Syriac Christian school moved to Edessa under Ephrem and was refounded about 489 by Narsai in Nisibis, with statutes about 496 that regulated life as a monastic university with a head, teachers and several hundred students, which taught the Bible commentaries of Theodore of Mopsuestia and was the main school of the Church of the East.
entries.note: Statutes of the School of Nisibis (trans. Vööbus, 1962); Adam Becker, Fear of God and the Beginning of Wisdom (2006).

entries.label: Procopius and the Persian wars
entries.hint: Procopius of Caesarea, legal adviser to Belisarius, wrote the Wars in eight books on the campaigns against the Persians, Vandals and Goths, the Buildings on Justinian's works and the Secret History, a hostile account of the court; his account of the Persian war of 527–553 and of Khusrau, and the account of the plague in 542, is the main source for the period.
entries.note: Procopius, Wars, Buildings, Secret History; Averil Cameron, Procopius and the Sixth Century (1985); Anthony Kaldellis, Procopius of Caesarea (2004).

entries.label: The Khwaday-namag and the royal annals
entries.hint: The Book of Kings (Khwaday-namag), a Middle Persian chronicle compiled under Khusrau I and Khusrau II from the oral lore of the Persian kings back to the legendary Kayanids and down to Yazdgerd III, which has not survived, was translated into Arabic by Ibn al-Muqaffa' in the eighth century and became the basis for Firdausi's Shahnameh and Tabari's account of the Persian kings.
entries.note: Ibn al-Muqaffa'; Tabari; Firdausi, Shahnameh; Daryaee 2009; Zeev Rubin.

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: The silk trade, Justinian's silkworms, the frontier tolls and the tribute paid to the Huns

entries.label: The tribute and the frontier trade
entries.hint: The treaties of 299 and 562 set out the places at which merchants could pass the frontier and the customs duties (the commercium), which the two states used to control the trade in silk, spices and precious stones; for the defence of the Caspian Gates Rome paid Persia for years, and the tribute and subsidies, which by 562 reached 30,000 solidi a year, were the main fiscal link between the empires.
entries.note: Peter the Patrician fr. 14; Menander fr. 6; Codex Justinianus 4.63.4; Greatrex and Lieu 2002.

entries.label: The Red Sea and the Indian trade
entries.loc: The Gulf and the Red Sea
entries.hint: The Persian Gulf and Red Sea trade, with Aksum on the Ethiopian coast as the Roman partner and the Persians' control of the ports of the Gulf and Ceylon (as Cosmas Indicopleustes notes in about 550), brought spices, pepper and ivory from India and Africa; the Sasanian conquest of Yemen about 570 was an attempt to control the southern end of the route.
entries.note: Cosmas Indicopleustes, Christian Topography; Procopius, Wars 1.19–20; Tabari; Daryaee 2009.

entries.label: Silk, the Persian monopoly and Justinian's silkworms
entries.hint: The Roman state, concerned at the price of silk, which came through Persia and Central Asia, limited the places of trade to Nisibis, Callinicum and Artaxata by the treaties from 408, and Justinian, who failed in 531 to open a route by Ethiopian traders, in 552 had two monks from Central Asia carry silkworm eggs hidden in hollow canes to Constantinople, which began an independent European silk industry.
entries.note: Procopius, Wars 8.17; Menander fr. 10; Theophanes of Byzantium; Codex Justinianus 4.63.4.

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: The Dara fortress, the Shushtar dams, siege warfare and Greek fire's ancestors

entries.label: The dams and weirs of Shushtar
entries.hint: The Band-e Kaisar, the Caesar's Dam, at Shushtar on the Karun, a weir of 500 metres with arches, a canal tunnel and a system of water mills that irrigated the plain of Khuzestan, is said by tradition to have been built by the Roman prisoners of Valerian's defeated army under Shapur I, and is a masterpiece of Roman hydraulic engineering in Persian service.
entries.note: Tabari; Ibn Hawqal; Daryaee 2009; Norman Smith, A History of Dams (1971); UNESCO World Heritage listing (2009).

entries.label: The fortress of Dara
entries.hint: Anastasius built, in the three years after the war of 502–506, a fortress city at Dara on the Mesopotamian frontier, 5 kilometres from Nisibis, with a double wall, a great defence tower, a dam and cisterns, and reconstructed it under Justinian; the Persians objected that it broke the treaties against building fortifications on the frontier, and its defeat of Persian assault in 530 under the general Belisarius (the battle of Dara) is the most famous action.
entries.note: Procopius, Wars 1.13–14, Buildings 2.1–3; Zacharias of Mytilene; Greatrex and Lieu 2002.

entries.label: Persian medicine and the games of the court
entries.hint: Under Khusrau I the physician Burzoe, who is said to have gone to India for the Panchatantra and brought back the game of chess (chatrang) and the book of Kalila and Dimna, translated into Middle Persian, was part of the cultural revival; Sasanian games of backgammon (nard) and chess entered the later Arabic world.
entries.note: Kalila wa Dimna; Burzoe's introduction (Shahnameh); Daryaee 2009; Harold Murray, A History of Chess (1913).

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: The Eternal Peace, the exchange of ambassadors, the Lakhmid and Ghassanid clients and the Red Sea trade

entries.label: The brotherhood of the two eyes
entries.hint: The Roman and Persian courts, in a tradition of mutual recognition and ritual, treated each other as the two lamps or eyes of the world and exchanged embassies at accessions with letters of brotherhood, such as Khusrau's to Maurice and Justin II's to Chosroes; the idea of the two empires as the two eyes of the world is in Persian and Greek sources of the fifth to seventh centuries.
entries.note: Menander fr. 6; Theophylact 4.11; Peter the Patrician fr. 13; Canepa 2009.

entries.label: The Hephthalites and the Persian-Roman Western Silk Road
entries.hint: The Hephthalites (White Huns), who held Bactria from about 440 and defeated and killed Peroz in 484, forced Persia to pay them tribute for decades, until Khusrau I, with the help of the Turkic Western Turks, destroyed them about 560, so bringing the Turks to the frontiers of Iran and sending their first embassies to Constantinople in 568.
entries.note: Procopius, Wars 1.3–4; Menander fr. 10; Étienne de la Vaissière, Sogdian Traders (2005); Daryaee 2009.

entries.label: Aksum, Himyar and the war over Yemen
entries.hint: The Jewish king of Himyar Dhu Nuwas persecuted the Christians of Najran in 523, and Kaleb of Aksum, at Justin I's request, invaded Yemen in 525; Abraha, the Aksumite governor, claimed the lordship in 540s, and Persian forces under Wahriz expelled the Ethiopians about 570, making Yemen a Sasanian province, and a prelude to the Prophet's Arabia.
entries.note: Procopius, Wars 1.19–20; Martyrdom of Arethas; Ibn Ishaq, Sira; Irfan Shahid, The Martyrs of Najran (1971).

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: The plague of Justinian, the dust-veil of 536 and the earthquakes of Antioch

entries.label: The deportations and the new cities
entries.hint: The Sasanian kings founded new cities and transported populations from the Roman provinces, among them the captives of Antioch in 256 and 540, who were settled at Gundeshapur and Veh Antiok Khusrau, of Apamea in 540 and of Dara in 573, with Christian and Greek-speaking communities that supplied the craftsmen of the royal works and a cause of the spread of Christianity in Persia.
entries.note: Procopius, Wars 2.9, 2.14; Shapur I, Res Gestae; Daryaee 2009; Morony 1984.

entries.label: The dust veil of 536 and the earthquakes of Antioch
entries.hint: The earthquake of 29 May 526 destroyed Antioch, killing, according to Malalas, 250,000 people, and the sun's dimming in 536, after a volcanic eruption, in the accounts of Procopius, John of Ephesus and Cassiodorus, brought a time of cold summers, crop failures and famine in the Mediterranean and Near East, which followed by plague in the 540s.
entries.note: Malalas 17.16; Procopius, Wars 4.14.5; Michael Baillie, Exodus to Arthur (1999); Ulf Büntgen et al., Nature Geoscience (2016).

entries.label: The plague of Justinian
entries.hint: Plague appeared at Pelusium in 541 and reached Constantinople in the spring of 542, where, according to Procopius, 10,000 a day died in the peak, and it spread through the Roman and Persian empires to the West, with deaths in the millions in the first outbreaks and returns for two centuries; Persia suffered too, and Khusrau I's army was weakened.
entries.note: Procopius, Wars 2.22–23; John of Ephesus; Evagrius 4.29; Lester Little (ed.), Plague and the End of Antiquity (2007); Peter Sarris.

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: The prisoners of Valerian, Shirin and Purandokht, the Persian martyrs and the soldiers of the frontier

entries.label: The soldiers and the dihqans
entries.hint: The Sasanian army was drawn from the dihqans, small landowners who furnished a mounted warrior with a retinue and lived in fortified villages, and from the Daylamite infantry and the Arab and Turkish auxiliaries; their numbers and the revenues which supported them were decided by Khusrau I's reform, and a part of them, as the Persian colonists in Yemen (the Abna), remained in the lands they had conquered.
entries.note: Tabari; Procopius, Wars 1.18; Pourshariati 2008; Daryaee 2009.

entries.label: The prisoners of Valerian
entries.hint: The tens of thousands of Roman soldiers and civilians taken by Shapur I were settled in Fars, Parthia and Khuzestan in cities he founded, and worked on his dams, bridges and palaces; some Greek and Syriac Christians and their descendants became the first communities of the Persian Church, among them the bishops of Gundeshapur and Bishapur.
entries.note: Res Gestae Divi Saporis; Zosimus 1.36; Morony 1984; Brock 1982.

entries.label: The Jews and Christians of the border cities
entries.hint: The towns of the frontier, such as Nisibis, Edessa, Dara and Amida, had Syriac-speaking Christian and Jewish populations that were of mixed loyalty and, in the war, were suspected by both empires; Jewish communities in the Galilee under Heraclius saw the Persian conquest of 614 as a possible release and afterwards suffered when Heraclius returned.
entries.note: Sebeos; Strategios; Doctrina Jacobi (c. 634); Kaegi 2003; Howard-Johnston 2010.

entries.label: Purandokht, Azarmidokht and the queens
entries.hint: After the murder of Kavad II's son Ardashir III by the general Shahrbaraz in 630, the daughters of Khusrau II, Purandokht (Boran) and Azarmidokht, were crowned as queens, struck coins in their own names and put the empire into some order for two years; Khusrau's queen Shirin, an Aramean Christian who built a monastery and is celebrated in the Persian poets, had been a power at the court.
entries.note: Tabari; Sebeos; coins of Boran and Azarmidokht; Daryaee 2009; Nizami, Khusrau and Shirin.
